Introduction.exp: WebAssembly (Wasm) is a binary instruction format for a stack-based virtual machine, designed as a portable compilation target for high-level languages like C, C++, and Rust. It enables near-native performance on the web by providing a low-level bytecode that browsers can decode and execute efficiently. Wasm modules are distributed as .wasm binary files or in the human-readable .wat text format. The core building blocks include functions, linear memory, tables, and globals, all structured within a (module) declaration. Wasm runs in a sandboxed environment with strong security guarantees, making it suitable for compute-intensive workloads like games, image processing, and scientific computing directly in the browser.
Introduction.code:
(module
  (func $add (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.add)
  (func $square (param $x i32) (result i32)
    local.get $x
    local.get $x
    i32.mul)
  (export "add" (func $add))
  (export "square" (func $square)))

Variables & Types.exp: WebAssembly provides four core numeric types: i32 (32-bit signed integer), i64 (64-bit signed integer), f32 (32-bit IEEE 754 floating point), and f64 (64-bit IEEE 754 floating point). Local variables are declared inside functions using (local $name type) after any parameters. Variables are zero-initialized and can be read with local.get and written with local.set. The local.tee instruction reads and writes in a single operation, leaving the value on the stack. Unlike high-level languages, Wasm does not have string, boolean, or object types — all complex data must be represented using these four numeric types and arranged in linear memory for data structures like arrays and strings.
Variables & Types.code:
(module
  (func $types (param $a i32) (param $b f64) (result f64)
    (local $c i32)
    (local $d f64)
    i32.const 42
    local.set $c
    f64.const 3.14
    local.set $d
    local.get $a
    f64.convert_i32_s
    local.get $b
    f64.add
    local.get $d
    f64.add)
  (export "types" (func $types)))

Operators.exp: WebAssembly provides typed arithmetic operators for each numeric type. i32 operations include add, sub, mul, div_s (signed division), div_u (unsigned), rem_s, rem_u, and bitwise and, or, xor, shl, shr_s, shr_u, rotl, rotr, clz, ctz, popcnt. Floating-point operations include f32.add, f32.sub, f32.mul, f32.div, f32.sqrt, f32.min, f32.max, f32.ceil, f32.floor, f32.trunc, f32.nearest, and f32.abs. Comparison operators return i32 (0 or 1): eq, ne, lt_s, lt_u, gt_s, gt_u, le_s, le_u, ge_s, ge_u. Type conversion operators like i32.wrap_i64, i64.extend_i32_s, f64.convert_i32_s allow casting between types. All operators are typed with the result type as a prefix.
Operators.code:
(module
  (func $arithmetic (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32 i32 i32 i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.add
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.sub
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.mul
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.div_s)
  (func $bitwise (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32 i32 i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.and
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.or
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.xor)
  (export "arithmetic" (func $arithmetic))
  (export "bitwise" (func $bitwise)))

Control Flow.exp: WebAssembly provides structured control flow instructions: block creates a labeled region that can be exited with br (branch); loop creates a label that branches backward for iteration; if/else/end provides conditional execution. The br instruction branches to a specific label by index (0 = innermost), br_if branches conditionally, and br_table provides computed jump dispatch. Unlike JavaScript's unstructured control flow, Wasm enforces structured control flow — every block must have a matching end, and the operand stack must be balanced at block boundaries. The return instruction exits the current function. Labels are indexed from the current depth outward, making nested control flow predictable and verifiable.
Control Flow.code:
(module
  (func $factorial (param $n i32) (result i32)
    (local $result i32)
    (local $i i32)
    local.get $n
    local.set $i
    i32.const 1
    local.set $result
    (block $done
      (loop $loop
        local.get $i
        i32.const 1
        i32.lt_s
        br_if $done
        local.get $result
        local.get $i
        i32.mul
        local.set $result
        local.get $i
        i32.const 1
        i32.sub
        local.set $i
        br $loop))
    local.get $result)
  (export "factorial" (func $factorial)))

Functions.exp: Functions in WebAssembly are defined with (func $name (param $p type) (result type) ...). Each function has a signature defined by its parameter types and return types. The multi-value proposal allows multiple return values, enabling tuple-like returns without memory writes. Functions can access local variables, global variables, and linear memory. Functions are exported with (export "name" (func $internal)) or imported from the host environment with (import "module" "name" (func ...)). Imported functions enable Wasm to call JavaScript APIs or WASI syscalls. Functions are called using the call instruction followed by the function name or index, providing direct and efficient dispatch.
Functions.code:
(module
  (func $add (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.add)
  (func $divmod (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32 i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.div_s
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.rem_s)
  (func $caller (export "caller") (param $x i32) (result i32)
    local.get $x
    i32.const 10
    call $add)
  (export "add" (func $add))
  (export "divmod" (func $divmod)))

Arrays & Collections.exp: WebAssembly does not have built-in array types — arrays are implemented using linear memory as a flat byte buffer. Elements are stored at calculated offsets and accessed with load/store instructions. A typical array of i32 values stores each element at address + index * 4. Wasm provides no bounds checking beyond the memory page limit, so array bounds must be checked manually. Multi-dimensional arrays are laid out in row-major or column-major order by calculating offsets. Structured collections like linked lists and trees are implemented by storing pointers (i32 addresses) to dynamically allocated memory regions. Memory growth via memory.grow enables dynamic resizing of collections at runtime.
Arrays & Collections.code:
(module
  (memory $mem 1)
  (func $store (param $base i32) (param $index i32) (param $value i32)
    local.get $base
    local.get $index
    i32.const 2
    i32.shl
    i32.add
    local.get $value
    i32.store)
  (func $load (param $base i32) (param $index i32) (result i32)
    local.get $base
    local.get $index
    i32.const 2
    i32.shl
    i32.add
    i32.load)
  (func $init
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 10
    i32.store
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 1
    i32.const 20
    i32.store
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 2
    i32.const 30
    i32.store)
  (export "store" (func $store))
  (export "load" (func $load))
  (export "init" (func $init))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

Strings.exp: WebAssembly has no native string type — strings are represented as byte sequences in linear memory, typically UTF-8 encoded. A string is stored as a contiguous block of bytes starting at a known memory address, optionally preceded by a length prefix or null-terminated. WASI provides fd_write for outputting strings via stdio. The JavaScript WebAssembly API can transfer strings by writing them to the Wasm module's memory buffer using TextEncoder and passing the address and length to Wasm functions. String operations like concatenation, comparison, substring extraction, and searching must be implemented manually in Wasm using byte-by-byte loops over memory regions.
Strings.code:
(module
  (memory $mem 1)
  (data (i32.const 0) "Hello, WebAssembly!")
  (data (i32.const 20) " from Kodex!")
  (func $strlen (param $addr i32) (result i32)
    (local $len i32)
    (local $byte i32)
    (block $done
      (loop $loop
        local.get $addr
        local.get $len
        i32.add
        i32.load8_u
        local.tee $byte
        i32.eqz
        br_if $done
        local.get $len
        i32.const 1
        i32.add
        local.set $len
        br $loop))
    local.get $len)
  (func $concat (param $dst i32) (param $src i32)
    local.get $src
    call $strlen
    local.get $dst
    local.get $src
    memory.copy)
  (export "strlen" (func $strlen))
  (export "concat" (func $concat))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

Maps & Dictionaries.exp: WebAssembly does not provide built-in map or dictionary types — they must be implemented manually using linear memory. A simple hash map stores key-value pairs in a contiguous array, using a hash function computed in Wasm to determine the bucket index. Open addressing with linear probing is a common collision resolution strategy. Each entry stores the key, value, and an occupancy flag. Memory must be managed carefully since keys and values are typically i32 integers, and string keys require additional buffer management. For small datasets, a flat array of key-value pairs with linear search is often simpler and faster than a full hash table in Wasm due to the absence of native hashing support.
Maps & Dictionaries.code:
(module
  (memory $mem 1)
  (global $entry_count (mut i32) (i32.const 0))
  (func $put (param $key i32) (param $value i32)
    (local $index i32)
    global.get $entry_count
    i32.const 3
    i32.shl
    local.set $index
    local.get $index
    local.get $key
    i32.store
    local.get $index
    i32.const 4
    i32.add
    local.get $value
    i32.store
    global.get $entry_count
    i32.const 1
    i32.add
    global.set $entry_count)
  (func $get (param $key i32) (result i32)
    (local $i i32)
    (local $idx i32)
    (block $done
      (loop $loop
        local.get $i
        global.get $entry_count
        i32.lt_s
        i32.eqz
        br_if $done
        local.get $i
        i32.const 3
        i32.shl
        local.tee $idx
        i32.load
        local.get $key
        i32.eq
        if
          local.get $idx
          i32.const 4
          i32.add
          i32.load
          return
        end
        local.get $i
        i32.const 1
        i32.add
        local.set $i
        br $loop))
    i32.const -1)
  (export "put" (func $put))
  (export "get" (func $get))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

Classes & Objects.exp: WebAssembly does not have native class or object support — the GC proposal adds struct and array types, but in core Wasm, objects are represented as data structures in linear memory. Each object is a contiguous block of bytes with fields at fixed offsets. A class-like pattern stores field offsets as constants and provides constructor, getter, and setter functions. Method dispatch can be implemented using function tables and call_indirect. The vtable pattern stores function pointers in a table with each object holding an index into the table. This mirrors how C++ compilers implement virtual functions when targeting Wasm via Emscripten.
Classes & Objects.code:
(module
  (memory $mem 1)
  (func $person_new (param $name_addr i32) (param $age i32) (result i32)
    (local $ptr i32)
    i32.const 0
    local.set $ptr
    local.get $ptr
    local.get $name_addr
    i32.store
    local.get $ptr
    i32.const 4
    i32.add
    local.get $age
    i32.store
    local.get $ptr)
  (func $person_get_age (param $ptr i32) (result i32)
    local.get $ptr
    i32.const 4
    i32.add
    i32.load)
  (func $person_set_age (param $ptr i32) (param $age i32)
    local.get $ptr
    i32.const 4
    i32.add
    local.get $age
    i32.store)
  (export "person_new" (func $person_new))
  (export "person_get_age" (func $person_get_age))
  (export "person_set_age" (func $person_set_age))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

Inheritance.exp: Inheritance in WebAssembly is implemented through manual composition and function table dispatch since Wasm has no native inheritance model. A base class struct occupies the first fields of a derived class struct, enabling pointer casting between base and derived types by using the same starting address. Virtual method dispatch uses call_indirect with a function table: each class stores a vtable index, and inherited methods are called by looking up the appropriate function reference by that index. Method overriding replaces a vtable entry with a new function. The elem section initializes the table with function references at instantiation time.
Inheritance.code:
(module
  (table $vtable 4 funcref)
  (elem (i32.const 0) $animal_speak $dog_speak $animal_run $dog_run)
  (type $speak (func (result i32)))
  (type $run (func (param i32) (result i32)))
  (memory $mem 1)
  (func $animal_speak (result i32)
    i32.const 0)
  (func $dog_speak (result i32)
    i32.const 1)
  (func $animal_run (param $dist i32) (result i32)
    local.get $dist)
  (func $dog_run (param $dist i32) (result i32)
    local.get $dist
    i32.const 2
    i32.mul)
  (func $animal_new (result i32)
    i32.const 0
    i32.store (i32.const 0)
    i32.const 0)
  (func $dog_new (result i32)
    i32.const 2
    i32.store (i32.const 0)
    i32.const 0)
  (func $speak (param $obj i32) (result i32)
    i32.const 0
    local.get $obj
    i32.load
    table.get $vtable
    call_indirect (type $speak))
  (export "animal_new" (func $animal_new))
  (export "dog_new" (func $dog_new))
  (export "speak" (func $speak))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

Interfaces.exp: Interfaces in WebAssembly are implemented using function tables and call_indirect for dynamic dispatch. An interface defines a set of function signatures (types), and implementations register their functions in a shared table at agreed-upon indices. The caller dispatches through the table using an index obtained from the object or passed as a parameter. This pattern is equivalent to COM interfaces, Go interfaces, or Rust trait objects. The type section defines the interface contracts, the table holds function references, and elem sections populate the table at instantiation. Components implementing the same interface must agree on the function index layout within their segment of the table.
Interfaces.code:
(module
  (type $drawable (func (param i32) (result i32)))
  (type $resizable (func (param i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (table $dispatch 4 funcref)
  (elem (i32.const 0) $circle_draw $rect_draw $circle_resize $rect_resize)
  (memory $mem 1)
  (func $circle_draw (param $radius i32) (result i32)
    local.get $radius
    i32.const 3
    i32.mul)
  (func $rect_draw (param $side i32) (result i32)
    local.get $side
    i32.const 4
    i32.mul)
  (func $circle_resize (param $r i32) (param $f i32) (result i32)
    local.get $r
    local.get $f
    i32.mul)
  (func $rect_resize (param $s i32) (param $f i32) (result i32)
    local.get $s
    local.get $f
    i32.mul)
  (func $draw (param $type i32) (param $val i32) (result i32)
    local.get $val
    i32.const 0
    local.get $type
    table.get $dispatch
    call_indirect (type $drawable))
  (func $resize (param $type i32) (param $val i32) (param $f i32) (result i32)
    local.get $val
    local.get $f
    i32.const 2
    local.get $type
    i32.add
    table.get $dispatch
    call_indirect (type $resizable))
  (export "draw" (func $draw))
  (export "resize" (func $resize))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

Exceptions.exp: The WebAssembly exception handling proposal adds try/catch blocks and typed exception tags to Wasm. Exception tags are declared with (tag $name (param types)) and thrown with the throw instruction. The try block opens a region that can catch exceptions, and the catch block matches specific tags or uses catch_all for any exception. The rethrow instruction re-throws a caught exception to the next handler. Exception handling enables Wasm to interoperate with C++ exceptions via Emscripten and JavaScript try/catch boundaries. Without the proposal, errors must be handled via return codes and explicit checking of each operation's result.
Exceptions.code:
(module
  (tag $div_by_zero (param))
  (func $safe_div (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    local.get $b
    i32.eqz
    if
      throw $div_by_zero
    end
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.div_s)
  (func $try_div (export "try_div") (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    block $handler (result i32)
      try (result i32)
        local.get $a
        local.get $b
        call $safe_div
      catch $div_by_zero
        i32.const 0
      end
    end)
  (export "safe_div" (func $safe_div)))

Debugging.exp: Debugging WebAssembly requires specialized tools since traditional debuggers cannot inspect Wasm execution directly. Chrome DevTools supports Wasm debugging with source maps, enabling breakpoints in the original C/Rust source code. Firefox provides WAT disassembly in the Debugger panel for stepping through instructions. The wabt toolkit offers wasm-objdump for inspecting module structure and wasm2wat for decompilation of binary modules. For WASI modules, wasmtime supports a --debug flag and wasminspect provides interactive debugging. Adding custom sections with DWARF debug info enables source-level debugging. The WASI logging proposal provides structured logging from within Wasm modules.
Debugging.code:
(module
  (import "env" "debug_log" (func $log (param i32)))
  (memory $mem 1)
  (data (i32.const 0) "debug: function entered")
  (data (i32.const 32) "debug: value = ")
  (func $debug_value (param $msg_addr i32) (param $val i32)
    local.get $msg_addr
    call $log
    local.get $val
    call $log)
  (func $compute (export "compute") (param $x i32) (result i32)
    i32.const 0
    call $log
    local.get $x
    i32.const 2
    i32.mul
    local.tee $x
    i32.const 32
    call $debug_value
    local.get $x)
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

File Operations.exp: File operations in WebAssembly require WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) for system-level access. WASI Preview 1 provides fd_write, fd_read, path_open, path_create_directory, path_unlink_file, path_filestat_get, and related syscalls. File access is capability-based — the host must explicitly grant filesystem access via --dir flags at runtime. The path_open syscall opens a file relative to a preopened directory (typically fd 3), returning a file descriptor for subsequent operations. Data is then read or written using fd_read and fd_write with iovec structures defined in linear memory. WASI Preview 2 introduces a stream-based model for more ergonomic file I/O with better error handling.
File Operations.code:
(module
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "fd_write"
    (func $fd_write (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "path_open"
    (func $path_open (param i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i64 i64 i32) (result i32)))
  (memory 1)
  (data (i32.const 0) "output.txt")
  (func $write_file (export "write_file")
    (local $fd i32)
    i32.const 3
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 11
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 0
    i64.const 0
    i64.const 0
    i32.const 100
    call $path_open
    local.set $fd
    i32.const 200
    i32.const 0
    i32.store
    i32.const 200
    i32.const 4
    i32.add
    i32.const 12
    i32.store
    local.get $fd
    i32.const 200
    i32.const 1
    i32.const 220
    call $fd_write
    drop)
  (export "memory" (memory 0)))

Input/Output.exp: Input and output in WebAssembly depend on the execution environment. In the browser, I/O happens through imported JavaScript functions that call DOM APIs, fetch, or WebSocket. In WASI environments, stdio uses fd_write for stdout (fd=1) and stderr (fd=2) and fd_read for stdin (fd=0). WASI uses iovec structures defined in linear memory — an array of {buf_ptr, buf_len} pairs that describe memory buffers. Output requires building a data buffer in memory and calling fd_write with the iovec. For efficient I/O, batch multiple writes into a single fd_write call using multiple iovec entries. The JavaScript WebAssembly API bridges browser I/O by passing callback functions in the import object during instantiation.
Input/Output.code:
(module
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "fd_write"
    (func $fd_write (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (memory 1)
  (data (i32.const 0) "Hello, WASI!\n")
  (data (i32.const 16) "Enter number: ")
  (func $print_str (param $addr i32) (param $len i32)
    i32.const 100
    local.get $addr
    i32.store
    i32.const 100
    i32.const 4
    i32.add
    local.get $len
    i32.store
    i32.const 1
    i32.const 100
    i32.const 1
    i32.const 108
    call $fd_write
    drop)
  (func $main (export "_start")
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 12
    call $print_str)
  (export "memory" (memory 0)))

Concurrency.exp: WebAssembly concurrency is enabled by the threads proposal, which adds SharedArrayBuffer-based shared memory and atomic operations. Shared memory is declared with the shared flag: (memory 1 10 shared). Atomic instructions like i32.atomic.load, i32.atomic.store, i32.atomic.rmw.add, i32.atomic.rmw.cmpxchg provide lock-free synchronization. The memory.atomic.wait and atomic.notify instructions implement futex-like synchronization primitives for blocking threads. Wasm threads are created via Web Workers in the browser — each worker instantiates the same Wasm module with a shared memory instance. Cross-instance communication happens through shared memory with well-defined memory ordering semantics.
Concurrency.code:
(module
  (memory $mem 1 10 shared)
  (global $counter (mut i32) (i32.const 0))
  (func $increment (export "increment")
    (local $expected i32)
    (block $done
      (loop $retry
        global.get $counter
        local.set $expected
        local.get $expected
        i32.const 1
        i32.add
        global.get $counter
        local.get $expected
        i32.atomic.rmw.cmpxchg (i32.const 0)
        local.get $expected
        i32.ne
        br_if $retry)))
  (func $get_counter (export "get_counter") (result i32)
    global.get $counter
    i32.atomic.load (i32.const 0))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

Modules.exp: WebAssembly modules are the fundamental unit of code organization and distribution. A module is a self-contained unit containing type definitions, function declarations, memory segments, tables, globals, imports, and exports. Modules can import functions, memories, tables, and globals from other modules or the host using (import "module" "name" ...). Exports make internal definitions available to consumers, forming the public API of the module. Dynamic linking between modules is achieved through shared memories and tables, enabling multi-module applications with separate compilation. The Component Model extends modules with typed WIT interfaces for better composition and interoperability between modules.
Modules.code:
(module
  (import "math" "add" (func $add (param i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (import "math" "memory" (memory $shared 1))
  (import "console" "log" (func $log (param i32)))
  (global $offset (import "config" "offset") i32)
  (func $compute (export "compute") (param $x i32) (result i32)
    local.get $x
    global.get $offset
    call $add
    local.tee $x
    call $log
    local.get $x)
  (export "compute" (func $compute)))

Best Practices.exp: Writing idiomatic and efficient WebAssembly requires understanding the stack machine model and memory model. Best practices include: minimizing call_indirect overhead by using direct calls when possible; keeping memory access patterns sequential for cache friendliness; using local variables instead of memory for temporary values; preferring i32 over i64 on 32-bit platforms; using bulk memory instructions (memory.copy, memory.fill) over manual byte loops; avoiding frequent JS-Wasm boundary crossings by batching work; compiling with -O3 and LTO for production; stripping debug sections from production builds; using streaming instantiation for faster loading; and validating all inputs to prevent out-of-bounds memory access.
Best Practices.code:
(module
  (memory $mem 1)
  (func $process (export "process") (param $data i32) (param $len i32) (result i32)
    (local $i i32)
    (local $sum i32)
    (block $done
      (loop $loop
        local.get $i
        local.get $len
        i32.ge_s
        br_if $done
        local.get $sum
        local.get $data
        local.get $i
        i32.const 2
        i32.shl
        i32.add
        i32.load
        i32.add
        local.set $sum
        local.get $i
        i32.const 1
        i32.add
        local.set $i
        br $loop))
    local.get $sum)
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

Performance.exp: Optimizing WebAssembly performance involves strategies across multiple dimensions. Memory optimization: align data to 8-byte boundaries, use Structure of Arrays (SoA) over Array of Structures (AoS) for better cache utilization, and minimize memory.grow calls. Computation optimization: use local variables instead of memory loads, prefer i32 operations over f64, use SIMD instructions (v128, i32x4, f32x4) for parallel work, and inline small hot functions. Binary size optimization: use -Oz, wasm-strip, and LTO for smaller modules. Load optimization: use streaming instantiation and split large modules into chunks. Threading: use shared memory with atomic operations for multi-core parallelism.
Performance.code:
(module
  (memory $mem 1)
  (func $sum_simd (export "sum_simd") (param $arr i32) (param $len i32) (result i32)
    (local $i i32)
    (local $sum v128)
    (local $total i32)
    v128.const i32x4 0 0 0 0
    local.set $sum
    (block $done
      (loop $loop
        local.get $i
        local.get $len
        i32.ge_s
        br_if $done
        local.get $sum
        local.get $arr
        local.get $i
        i32.const 2
        i32.shl
        i32.add
        v128.load
        i32x4.add
        local.set $sum
        local.get $i
        i32.const 4
        i32.add
        local.set $i
        br $loop))
    local.get $sum
    i32x4.extract_lane 0
    local.get $sum
    i32x4.extract_lane 1
    i32.add
    local.get $sum
    i32x4.extract_lane 2
    i32.add
    local.get $sum
    i32x4.extract_lane 3
    i32.add)
  (export "memory" (memory $mem)))

What is WebAssembly: WebAssembly (Wasm) is a binary instruction format for a stack-based virtual machine. It is designed as a portable compilation target for programming languages, enabling deployment on the web for client and server applications with near-native performance.

(module
  (func (export "add") (param i32 i32) (result i32)
    local.get 0
    local.get 1
    i32.add)
  (func (export "square") (param i32) (result i32)
    local.get 0
    local.get 0
    i32.mul)
)
Wasm vs JavaScript: WebAssembly is not a replacement for JavaScript — they are complementary. JS handles DOM, events, and high-level logic while Wasm runs compute-intensive tasks (games, video processing, cryptography) at near-native speed. JS loads Wasm modules and calls their exported functions.
Use Cases: WebAssembly excels at: gaming (Unity/Unreal export to Wasm), image/video processing (FFmpeg.wasm), audio synthesis, CAD/3D modeling, scientific computing, cryptocurrency (Polkadot uses Wasm for runtime), plugin systems (Extism), edge computing (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute@Edge), and server-side code sandboxing.
Browser Support: WebAssembly is supported in all modern browsers (Chrome 57+, Firefox 52+, Safari 11+, Edge 16+). The Wasm spec is a W3C standard. New proposals (SIMD, threads, GC, exceptions) are progressively rolling out across browsers. Check caniuse.com and webassembly.org/features for current status.
WASI Overview: WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) extends Wasm beyond the browser to server environments. It provides a POSIX-like API for filesystem, networking, clock, and random number access. WASI enables running Wasm as a portable runtime on servers, edge, and embedded devices with strong sandboxing.

# Running a WASI module with wasmtime
wasmtime --dir=. myapp.wasm arg1 arg2

# Environment variables
wasmtime --env KEY=VALUE myapp.wasm

# List available WASI preview2 features
wasmtime --wasm feature-list

WAT Syntax Basics: WAT (WebAssembly Text Format) is a human-readable representation of Wasm binary. Files use `.wat` extension. A module is an S-expression tree with `(module ...)` as root. Keywords include `func`, `param`, `result`, `local`, `memory`, `table`, `import`, `export`, `global`.
Functions and Parameters: Functions are defined with `(func $name (param $p type) (result type) ...)`. Parameters are referenced by name or index. Multiple return values are allowed. Functions can be exported with `(export "name" (func $internal))` or imported from the host.

(module
  (func $add (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.add)
  (func $double (param i32) (result i32)
    local.get 0
    local.get 0
    i32.add)
  (export "add" (func $add))
  (export "double" (func $double))
)
Local Variables: Local variables are declared with `(local $name type)` after parameters. They are zero-initialized. Use `local.get $name` to read and `local.set $name` to write. `local.tee $name` reads and writes in one operation (useful for keeping a value on the stack).

(module
  (func $example (param $x i32) (result i32)
    (local $y i32)
    (local $z i32)
    i32.const 10
    local.set $y
    local.get $x
    local.get $y
    i32.add
    local.tee $z
    local.get $z
    i32.add
  )
  (export "example" (func $example))
)
Control Flow: Wasm provides `block`, `loop`, `if`, `else`, `end` for control flow. `block` exits with `br N` (0 = innermost). `loop` branches back with `br N`. `br_if` conditionally branches. `br_table` is a computed jump. `return` exits the current function. All branches must target a valid label.

(module
  (func $factorial (param $n i32) (result i32)
    (local $result i32)
    (local $i i32)
    local.get $n
    local.set $i
    i32.const 1
    local.set $result
    (block $done
      (loop $loop
        local.get $i
        i32.const 1
        i32.lt_s
        br_if $done
        local.get $result
        local.get $i
        i32.mul
        local.set $result
        local.get $i
        i32.const 1
        i32.sub
        local.set $i
        br $loop))
    local.get $result)
  (export "factorial" (func $factorial))
)
Memory Operations: Linear memory is a contiguous byte array accessed with `load` and `store` instructions. Memory is declared with `(memory $name pages)`. One page = 64KiB. Load/store variants: `i32.load`, `i64.load`, `f32.load`, `f64.load`, `i32.load8_s/u`, `i32.store`, `i64.store`, `i32.store8`. Memory grows via `memory.grow`.

(module
  (memory $mem 1)
  (func $store (param $addr i32) (param $value i32)
    local.get $addr
    local.get $value
    i32.store)
  (func $load (param $addr i32) (result i32)
    local.get $addr
    i32.load)
  (export "memory" (memory $mem))
  (export "store" (func $store))
  (export "load" (func $load))
)
Numeric Types: Wasm supports four numeric types: `i32` (32-bit integer), `i64` (64-bit integer), `f32` (32-bit float IEEE 754), `f64` (64-bit float IEEE 754). Each type has arithmetic (`add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div_s/u`, `rem_s/u`), comparison (`eq`, `ne`, `lt_s/u`, `gt_s/u`, `le_s/u`, `ge_s/u`), and conversion operations.

(module
  (func $mixed (param $a i32) (param $b f64) (result f64)
    local.get $a
    f64.convert_i32_s
    local.get $b
    f64.mul)
  (func $min (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.lt_s
    if (result i32)
      local.get $a
    else
      local.get $b
    end)
  (export "mixed" (func $mixed))
  (export "min" (func $min))
)

Linear Memory Model: Wasm memory is a simple flat byte array with no address space layout randomization. It starts at a configured initial size and can grow up to a maximum. Memory is sandboxed — Wasm code cannot access memory outside its allocated buffer. All memory access is bounds-checked at runtime.

(module
  (memory $mem 1 256)
  (func $init
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 42
    i32.store
    i32.const 4
    i32.const 100
    i32.store
    i32.const 8
    i32.const 200
    i64.store)
  (func $grow (param $pages i32) (result i32)
    local.get $pages
    memory.grow)
  (export "init" (func $init))
  (export "grow" (func $grow))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem))
)
Tables and Call Indirect: Tables are arrays of function references (or other reference types). `call_indirect` enables dynamic dispatch by calling a function from a table by index. Tables are typed by function signature. `elem` sections pre-populate tables. This enables virtual tables, callbacks, and dynamic linking.

(module
  (table $funcs 2 funcref)
  (elem (i32.const 0) $add $sub)
  (func $add (param i32 i32) (result i32)
    local.get 0 local.get 1 i32.add)
  (func $sub (param i32 i32) (result i32)
    local.get 0 local.get 1 i32.sub)
  (func $dispatch (param $op i32) (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.const 0
    local.get $op
    table.get $funcs
    call_indirect (result i32))
  (export "dispatch" (func $dispatch))
  (export "funcs" (table $funcs))
)
Imports and Exports: Wasm modules can import functions, memories, tables, and globals from the host environment using `(import "module" "name" ...)`. Exports make internal definitions available outside the module. This is the primary mechanism for Wasm-JS interop and dynamic linking between Wasm modules.
Global Variables: Globals are module-scoped variables declared with `(global $name type value)`. Mutable globals use `(mut type)`. `global.get` and `global.set` access them. Immutable globals can be exported or imported. Mutable globals cannot be exported from the host in the core spec (but can in some extensions).

(module
  (global $counter (mut i32) (i32.const 0))
  (global $PI f64 (f64.const 3.14159))
  (func $increment
    global.get $counter
    i32.const 1
    i32.add
    global.set $counter)
  (func $get_counter (result i32)
    global.get $counter)
  (export "increment" (func $increment))
  (export "get_counter" (func $get_counter))
  (export "PI" (global $PI))
)
Stack Machine Model: Wasm is a stack machine — instructions push values onto an operand stack and consume values from it. `i32.const 5` pushes 5. `i32.add` pops two values, adds them, pushes result. There is also a control stack for blocks/loops/if. Structured control flow ensures the stack is balanced at each block boundary.

;; Stack trace for: (i32.const 3) (i32.const 4) (i32.add) (i32.const 2) (i32.mul)
;; Step 1: push 3        Stack: [3]
;; Step 2: push 4        Stack: [3, 4]
;; Step 3: i32.add       Stack: [7]      (pops 3+4, pushes 7)
;; Step 4: push 2        Stack: [7, 2]
;; Step 5: i32.mul       Stack: [14]     (pops 7*2, pushes 14)

(module
  (func $calc (result i32)
    i32.const 3
    i32.const 4
    i32.add
    i32.const 2
    i32.mul)
  (export "calc" (func $calc))
)
Module Structure: A Wasm module has sections: Type (function signatures), Function (function declarations), Code (function bodies), Memory, Table, Global, Export, Import, Element, Data, Custom (debug names, source maps). Sections appear in a specific order in the binary format. The module is validated before instantiation.

(module
  ;; Type section (function signatures)
  (type $sig (func (param i32 i32) (result i32)))
  ;; Import section
  (import "js" "log" (func $log (param i32)))
  ;; Function section
  (func $add (type $sig)
    local.get 0
    local.get 1
    i32.add)
  ;; Memory section
  (memory $mem 1)
  ;; Data section
  (data (i32.const 0) "Hello")
  ;; Export section
  (export "add" (func $add))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem))
)

C to Wasm with Emscripten: Emscripten compiles C/C++ to Wasm using LLVM + Binaryen. Install via emsdk. `emcc` replaces gcc/clang. Output is a .wasm file plus JavaScript glue code. Flags: `-O3` (optimize), `-s WASM=1` (Wasm output), `-s EXPORTED_FUNCTIONS` (control exports), `-s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH`.
Rust to Wasm with wasm-pack: wasm-pack is the official tool for building Rust→Wasm packages. Install with `cargo install wasm-pack`. Create a library with `--lib` type = `cdylib`. Use `wasm-bindgen` for JS interop. Build with `wasm-pack build --target web` (browser) or `--target nodejs` (Node) or `--target bundler`.
AssemblyScript: AssemblyScript is a TypeScript-like language that compiles directly to Wasm. It is ideal for JS developers wanting to write Wasm without learning Rust/C++. Install via npm. Use `asc` compiler. Provides strict typing, manual memory management, and near-Wasm-level control with JS-like syntax.
Go to Wasm with TinyGo: TinyGo is a Go compiler for microcontrollers and Wasm. It produces smaller binaries than the standard Go compiler. Use `GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm` with standard Go (1.21+) for WASI support. TinyGo supports a broader set of Go features in Wasm. For browser: `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build`.
WAT to Wasm with wat2wasm: The wabt (WebAssembly Binary Toolkit) provides `wat2wasm` to compile WAT to binary .wasm format. `wasm2wat` does the reverse (decompile). `wasm-validate` checks validity. `wasm-objdump` inspects sections. `wasm-strip` removes debug sections. `wasm-opt` (from Binaryen) optimizes Wasm binaries.

# Install wabt (pre-built binaries or build from source)
# https://github.com/WebAssembly/wabt

# Compile WAT to Wasm binary
wat2wasm input.wat -o output.wasm

# Decompile Wasm to WAT
wasm2wat output.wasm -o decompiled.wat

# Validate a Wasm module
wasm-validate output.wasm

# Inspect sections
wasm-objdump -x output.wasm
Zig to Wasm: Zig has first-class WebAssembly support as a compilation target. Use `-target wasm32-freestanding` for browser Wasm (no system deps) or `-target wasm32-wasi` for WASI. Zig's comptime features make it highly expressive for Wasm. Zig can produce tiny Wasm binaries with no runtime overhead.

What is WASI: WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) is a modular system interface standard for WebAssembly outside the browser. It provides capabilities-based security — each program only has access to resources explicitly granted. WASI Preview 1 is stable (based on POSIX-like syscalls). Preview 2 introduces the Component Model and wit IDL.

# WASI Preview 1 execution
wasmtime --dir=/sandbox --env DB_PATH=/data/db app.wasm

# Allow specific directories
wasmtime --dir=. --dir=/tmp app.wasm

# Pass environment variables
wasmtime --env LOG_LEVEL=debug --env HOME=/home/user app.wasm
WASI Preview 1: WASI Preview 1 defines ~40 syscalls for: args, environ, clock, fd (file descriptor) read/write/seek, path operations, random, and process exit. It uses the `wasi_unstable` or `wasi_snapshot_preview1` module name. Preview 1 modules use a linear memory for I/O with explicit pointer+length parameters.

(module
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "fd_write"
    (func $fd_write (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (memory 1)
  (data (i32.const 0) "Hello WASI!\n")
  (func (export "_start")
    (local $ret i32)
    ;; iov = { buf=0, len=12 }
    i32.const 12
    i32.store (i32.const 16)
    i32.const 0
    i32.store (i32.const 12)
    i32.const 1
    i32.const 12
    i32.const 20
    call $fd_write
    drop)
)
WASI Preview 2 and Component Model: WASI Preview 2 replaces the POSIX-like syscall interface with the Component Model. Components use WIT (Wasm Interface Types) IDL to define typed interfaces. Components can be composed without runtime overhead. Preview 2 introduces streams, async, and richer types (strings, lists, records, variants).

# Component Model toolchain
# Generate Wasm component from Rust:
cargo install wasm-tools
cargo install wit-bindgen-cli

# Create a WIT interface
# packages/my-app/my-app.wit
# package my-app;
# interface types {
#   record user { name: string, age: u32 }
# }

# Build with component target:
# wasm-tools component new my-module.wasm -o my-component.wasm

# Run a component:
# wasmtime run my-component.wasm
fd_write and stdio: The `fd_write` syscall is the primary output mechanism in WASI Preview 1. It takes (fd, iovs_ptr, iovs_len, ret_ptr). fd 1 = stdout, fd 2 = stderr. iovs (io vectors) are `{buf_ptr, buf_len}` pairs. WASI handles multiple iovs efficiently. The `_start` function is the module entry point (like main).

(module
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "fd_write"
    (func $fd_write (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "fd_read"
    (func $fd_read (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (memory 1)
  (data (i32.const 0) "Enter name: ")
  (export "_start" (func $_start))
  (func $_start
    ;; write prompt
    i32.const 1
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 12
    i32.const 100
    call $fd_write
    drop
    ;; read input
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 200
    i32.const 12
    i32.const 100
    call $fd_read
    drop)
)
Filesystem Access in WASI: WASI provides filesystem operations via `path_open`, `fd_read`, `fd_write`, `fd_close`, `path_create_directory`, `path_unlink_file`, `path_filestat_get`, and others. Directories must be preopened (granted at runtime via `--dir`). The first preopened directory typically gets fd 3. Capabilities-based security means only explicitly granted paths are accessible.

# Grant filesystem access
wasmtime --dir=/data --dir=/tmp myapp.wasm

# Grant only read access to a directory
wasmtime --dir=/readonly::/data myapp.wasm

# Run with no filesystem access (default)
wasmtime myapp.wasm

# List available preopens inside Wasm:
// WASI fd_prestat_get and fd_prestat_dir_name
Running Wasm with wasmtime CLI: Wasmtime is the most popular standalone Wasm runtime. It supports WASI Preview 1 and Preview 2, can run WAT files directly, and provides security sandboxing via `--dir` (filesystem), `--env` (env vars), and resource limits. Use `wasmtime --help` for all options. `wasmtime serve` runs HTTP handlers as Wasm components.

# Run a WAT file directly
wasmtime hello.wat

# Run compiled Wasm with WASI
wasmtime --dir=. --env NAME=World myapp.wasm

# Fuel metering (limit execution)
wasmtime --fuel 1000 myapp.wasm

# Cache compiled code
wasmtime --cache myapp.wasm

# List all WASI capabilities
wasmtime wasmtime-flags

# Time and memory limits
wasmtime --max-memory=10M --max-instructions=100000 myapp.wasm

SIMD Instructions: WebAssembly SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data, proposal) enables parallel operations on 128-bit vectors.  instruction prefix `i8x16`, `i16x8`, `i32x4`, `i64x2`, `f32x4`, `f64x2`. Operations include add, sub, mul, shuffle, blend, min, max, compare, load_splat, and more. SIMD can accelerate multimedia, cryptography, and scientific code 2-4x.

(module
  (func $dot_product
    (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (param $n i32) (result f32)
    (local $sum f32)
    (local $i i32)
    (local $va v128) (local $vb v128) (local $vmul v128)
    loop $loop
      local.get $i
      local.get $n
      i32.ge_s
      if $done
        local.get $a
        local.get $i
        i32.add
        v128.load
        local.set $va
        local.get $b
        local.get $i
        i32.add
        v128.load
        local.set $vb
        local.get $va
        local.get $vb
        f32x4.mul
        local.get $vmul
        f32x4.add
        local.set $vmul
        local.get $i
        i32.const 16
        i32.add
        local.set $i
        br $loop)
    local.get $vmul
    f32x4.extract_lane 0
    local.get $vmul
    f32x4.extract_lane 1
    f32.add
    local.get $vmul
    f32x4.extract_lane 2
    f32.add
    local.get $vmul
    f32x4.extract_lane 3
    f32.add)
  (export "dot_product" (func $dot_product))
)
Multi-value Returns: The multi-value proposal allows functions to return multiple values (not just one). This enables tuple returns, multiple outputs without memory, and more expressive APIs. Blocks can also yield multiple values. Multi-value enables natural composition without temporary memory writes.

(module
  (func $divmod (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32 i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.div_s
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.rem_s)
  (func $use_divmod
    i32.const 17
    i32.const 5
    call $divmod
    ;; stack now has [3, 2]  (quotient, remainder)
    drop
    drop)
  (export "divmod" (func $divmod))
)
Bulk Memory Operations: Bulk memory (memcpy, memset, memmove) operations are Wasm instructions for fast memory copying and filling. `memory.copy` (dst, src, len) copies memory regions. `memory.fill` (addr, val, len) fills memory with a byte. `table.copy`, `table.init`, `elem.drop` for tables. These replace manual loops with native-speed operations.

(module
  (memory $mem 1)
  (data (i32.const 0) "Hello, World!")
  (func $copy_and_fill
    ;; Copy bytes from offset 0 to offset 100, length 13
    i32.const 100
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 13
    memory.copy
    ;; Fill bytes at offset 0 with 0xFF, length 10
    i32.const 0
    i32.const 0xFF
    i32.const 10
    memory.fill)
  (func $check (param $addr i32) (result i32)
    local.get $addr
    i32.load8_u)
  (export "copy_and_fill" (func $copy_and_fill))
  (export "check" (func $check))
  (export "memory" (memory $mem))
)
Reference Types: Reference types extend Wasm with `funcref` (function references) and `externref` (opaque host references). `funcref` enables dynamic function calls via tables. `externref` allows Wasm to hold JS/DOM objects without copying. The GC proposal extends this with struct/array `i31ref`. Reference types enable richer interop patterns.

(module
  (table $handlers funcref (elem $handle_click $handle_hover))
  (func $handle_click (param i32) (result i32)
    i32.const 1)
  (func $handle_hover (param i32) (result i32)
    i32.const 2)
  (func $dispatch (param $idx i32) (param $evt i32) (result i32)
    local.get $evt
    i32.const 0
    local.get $idx
    table.get $handlers
    call_indirect (param i32) (result i32))
  (export "dispatch" (func $dispatch))
  (export "handlers" (table $handlers))
)
Exception Handling: The exception handling proposal adds `try`, `catch`, `throw`, `rethrow` to Wasm. Exception tags are declared with `(tag $name (param types))`. `try` blocks can catch specific tags. `catch_all` handles any exception. This enables Wasm modules to interoperate with JS exceptions and C++ try/catch.

(module
  (tag $oob (param i32))
  (func $risky (param $index i32) (param $len i32) (result i32)
    local.get $index
    local.get $len
    i32.ge_u
    if
      local.get $index
      throw $oob
    end
    i32.const 42)
  (func $safe_get (param $index i32) (param $len i32) (result i32)
    block $handler (result i32)
      try (result i32)
        local.get $index
        local.get $len
        call $risky
      catch $oob
        i32.const -1
      end
    end)
  (export "safe_get" (func $safe_get))
  (export "oob" (tag $oob))
)
Garbage Collection: Wasm GC adds heap-allocated structs, arrays, and `i31ref` (31-bit integers stored inline). Enables languages with GC (Java, Kotlin, Dart, Swift) to compile to Wasm efficiently. `struct.new`, `struct.get`, `struct.set`, `array.new`, `array.get`, `array.len`. Combined with reference types, GC makes Wasm a universal compilation target.

(module
  (type $point (struct (field $x i32) (field $y i32)))
  (type $point_arr (array (ref $point)))
  (func $make_point (param $x i32) (param $y i32) (result (ref $point))
    (struct.new $point
      (local.get $x)
      (local.get $y)))
  (func $distance_sq (param $p (ref $point)) (result i32)
    (local $dx i32)
    (local $dy i32)
    (struct.get $point $x (local.get $p))
    (struct.get $point $x (local.get $p))
    i32.mul
    (struct.get $point $y (local.get $p))
    (struct.get $point $y (local.get $p))
    i32.mul
    i32.add)
  (export "make_point" (func $make_point))
  (export "distance_sq" (func $distance_sq))
)

Memory Layout Optimization: Efficient memory layout reduces cache misses and binary size. Strategies: align data to 4/8 byte boundaries, pack small fields, use i32/i64 instead of variable-length, reuse memory buffers, avoid fragmentation with arena allocators, prefer stack over heap, use `memory.fill` for zeroing, and keep working set small to stay in Wasm's 64KiB pages.

;; Poor layout (wasteful)
;; struct { i32 id, i64 ts, i32 flag, i64 val }
;; 24 bytes per entry

;; Better layout (packed)
;; struct { i32 id, i32 flag, i64 ts, i64 val }
;; 20 bytes per entry

;; Best for hot path (cache-friendly)
;; Separate arrays: ids[], flags[], timestamps[], values[]
;; Sequential access patterns maximize cache utilization

(module
  (memory $mem 10)
  (func $store_point (param $addr i32) (param $x i32) (param $y i32)
    local.get $addr
    local.get $x
    i32.store
    local.get $addr
    i32.const 4
    i32.add
    local.get $y
    i32.store)
  (export "store_point" (func $store_point))
)
Reducing Binary Size: Smaller Wasm modules load faster. Techniques: use `-Oz` (optimize for size), strip debug sections (`wasm-strip`), avoid unused exports, use LTO (link-time optimization), compress with gzip/brotli (Wasm compresses well, often 50-70% reduction), merge identical functions, and prefer integer operations over floating-point.

# Optimize for size with various tools

# Emscripten
emcc -Oz -s WASM=1 -s EXPORTED_FUNCTIONS='["_main"]' -o out.js input.c

# Rust (add to Cargo.toml)
# [profile.release]
# opt-level = 'z'   # Optimize for size
# lto = true         # Link-time optimization
# strip = true       # Strip symbols

# Binaryen optimizer
wasm-opt -Oz input.wasm -o output.wasm

# Strip custom sections
wasm-strip input.wasm -o output.wasm

# Final size check
ls -lh output.wasm
gzip -c output.wasm | wc -c
Compiler Optimization Flags: Compiler optimizations greatly impact Wasm performance. GCC/Clang: `-O2` (balanced), `-O3` (aggressive), `-Ofast` (fastest, may break standards). Rust: `opt-level = 3`, `lto = true`, `codegen-units = 1`. Emscripten: `-O3 -s WASM=1`. Binaryen: `wasm-opt -O4`. Key flags produce 2-5x speed improvements over unoptimized code.

# C with Emscripten optimization levels
# -O0: No optimization (fastest compile, slowest code)
emcc -O0 -s WASM=1 -o out.js input.c

# -O1: Simple optimizations
emcc -O1 -s WASM=1 -o out.js input.c

# -O2: Standard optimizations (good balance)
emcc -O2 -s WASM=1 -o out.js input.c

# -O3: Aggressive inlining and vectorization
emcc -O3 -s WASM=1 -o out.js input.c

# -Oz: Optimize for size (smallest binary)
emcc -Oz -s WASM=1 -o out.js input.c

# -Os: Optimize for size (less aggressive than Oz)
emcc -Os -s WASM=1 -o out.js input.c
Profiling Wasm Execution: Profiling identifies bottlenecks. Browser DevTools support Wasm profiling in Chrome (Performance panel shows Wasm functions in flamecharts). Wasmtime has `--profile=jitdump` for perf Linux profiler. Binaryen's `wasm-opt --profile` analyzes function hotness. Key metrics: instruction count, memory access patterns, call frequency.

# Profiling with Chrome DevTools
# 1. Open DevTools → Performance
# 2. Record while running Wasm
# 3. Look for WebAssembly entries in flame chart
# 4. Click Wasm functions to see source info (if debug sections present)

# Profiling with wasmtime on Linux
wasmtime --profile=jitdump myapp.wasm
perf record -k 1 -e instructions:u ./myapp.wasm
perf report

# Count instructions
wasmtime --fuel 1000000000 myapp.wasm 2>&1 | tail

# Binaryen optimization info
wasm-opt --print-features input.wasm
Benchmarking Wasm vs Native: When benchmarking Wasm vs native: compare apples-to-apples (same algorithm), account for Wasm's sandbox overhead (bounds checks), test different optimization levels, measure cold vs warm starts, track memory usage, consider Wasm's 32-bit address space limit, and use realistic workloads. Wasm typically achieves 60-90% of native speed for compute-heavy tasks.

# Performance comparison template
# 1. Write same algorithm in C/Rust
# 2. Compile natively: gcc -O3 -o native prog.c
# 3. Compile to Wasm: emcc -O3 -s WASM=1 -o prog.js prog.c
# 4. Benchmark native:
time ./native

# 5. Benchmark Wasm in wasmtime:
time wasmtime prog.wasm

# 6. Benchmark Wasm in browser:
// performance.now() before and after

# Typical results (compute-heavy):
# Native:  100ms
# Wasmtime: ~120ms (83% of native)
# Browser:  ~140ms (71% of native)
Streaming Compilation: WebAssembly supports streaming compilation via `WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming()`. This starts compiling as soon as the first bytes arrive, overlapping download and compile time. For large modules, this can halve total load time. Wasmtime also supports streaming via `--stream`. Binary format is designed for single-pass compilation.

Image Processing with Wasm: Image processing benefits greatly from Wasm's performance. Libraries like libvips, stb_image, and libpng can be compiled to Wasm. Operations like resize, blur, filter, and format conversion run at near-native speed. Squoosh.app (by Google) uses Wasm for image compression. Web workers keep the UI responsive.
Audio Synthesis and Processing: WebAssembly enables real-time audio synthesis and processing in browsers. Libraries like FAUST (functional audio synthesis) compile to Wasm. Use AudioWorklet for audio thread execution. Wasm excels at FFT, convolution reverb, spectral processing, and waveform generation. Latency can be as low as 2-3ms.
Game Engines with Wasm: Unity and Unreal Engine both support WebAssembly exports. Unity uses WebGL 2.0 + Wasm for browser builds. Unreal uses Emscripten to compile C++ to Wasm. Godot has a Wasm export template. Browser games can now achieve console-quality graphics. Performance is within 10-30% of native with proper optimization.
Scientific Computing: Wasm enables complex scientific computing in browsers. TensorFlow.js uses Wasm backend for ML inference. BLAS/LAPACK linear algebra routines compile well to Wasm. NumPy-like operations, FFT, PDE solvers, and Monte Carlo simulations run efficiently. Workers enable parallel computation without blocking UI.
Blockchain and Smart Contracts: Several blockchain platforms use Wasm for smart contracts: Polkadot/Substrate (wasm runtime), EOS, Cosmos, Internet Computer. Wasm provides deterministic execution (same code, same result everywhere), sandboxed environment, and flexible gas metering. Smart contract SDKs provide Wasm toolchains for Rust and AssemblyScript.
Plugin Systems with Extism: Extism is a framework for building pluggable systems using WebAssembly. Host applications (Go, Rust, JS, Python, etc.) load Wasm plugins that extend functionality safely. Plugins can be loaded from files, URLs, or registries. Each plugin runs in its own sandbox with configurable resource limits.

WAT Syntax Deep Dive: WebAssembly Text Format (WAT) is the human-readable representation of WebAssembly. WAT uses S-expressions (Lisp-like parentheses) to define modules, functions, and instructions. A WAT file starts with a (module) declaration. Functions are defined with (func), parameters with (param), return types with (result), and local variables with (local). WebAssembly instructions are typed and use structured control flow. WAT is used for reading compiler output, debugging, and writing optimized wasm modules by hand.

(module
  ;; Import a function from JavaScript
  (import "console" "log" (func $log (param i32)))
  
  ;; Export a function to JavaScript
  (func $add (export "add") (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.add
  )
  
  ;; Export a function that calls imported log
  (func (export "run")
    i32.const 42
    call $log
  )
)
WAT Instructions & Stack Machine: WebAssembly is a stack-based virtual machine. Instructions push values onto an operand stack or pop values and perform operations. Basic instructions: i32.const, i64.const, f32.const, f64.const push constants. local.get, local.set, local.tee access local variables. global.get, global.set access global variables. i32.add, i32.sub, i32.mul are arithmetic operators. i32.load, i32.store access linear memory. call invokes functions. block, loop, if/else/end provide structured control flow.

(module
  (func $factorial (export "factorial") (param $n i32) (result i32)
    ;; if n <= 1 return 1
    (if (result i32) (i32.le_s (local.get $n) (i32.const 1))
      (then (i32.const 1))
      (else
        ;; n * factorial(n - 1)
        (i32.mul
          (local.get $n)
          (call $factorial (i32.sub (local.get $n) (i32.const 1)))
        )
      )
    )
  )
  
  ;; Loop-based factorial (no recursion)
  (func $factorial_loop (export "factorial_loop") (param $n i32) (result i32)
    (local $result i32)
    (local.set $result (i32.const 1))
    (block $done
      (loop $loop
        ;; if n == 0, break
        (br_if $done (i32.eqz (local.get $n)))
        ;; result *= n
        (local.set $result (i32.mul (local.get $result) (local.get $n)))
        ;; n -= 1
        (local.set $n (i32.sub (local.get $n) (i32.const 1)))
        ;; continue loop
        (br $loop)
      )
    )
    (local.get $result)
  )
)
WAT Memory & Tables: WebAssembly modules can have linear memory and tables. (memory) defines a contiguous array of bytes starting at 0 — initial size in pages (64KB each), optionally with a maximum size. data sections initialize memory with bytes at a given offset. Memory can be shared between wasm and JavaScript. (table) defines an array of function references for indirect calls (call_indirect). Tables enable function pointers and dynamic dispatch. (elem) sections initialize table entries. Use memory.grow to dynamically increase memory at runtime.

(module
  ;; Define 1 page (64KB) of linear memory, max 256 pages
  (memory (export "memory") 1 256)
  
  ;; Initialize memory with string data
  (data (i32.const 0) "Hello from WebAssembly!")
  
  ;; Function table for indirect calls
  (table (export "table") 2 funcref)
  (elem (i32.const 0) $add $subtract)
  
  (func $add (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.add
  )
  
  (func $subtract (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    local.get $a
    local.get $b
    i32.sub
  )
  
  ;; Indirect call through table
  (func $compute (export "compute") (param $op i32) (param $a i32) (param $b i32) (result i32)
    (call_indirect (type $arith) (local.get $a) (local.get $b) (local.get $op))
  )
  
  (type $arith (func (param i32 i32) (result i32)))
)
Compiling C/Rust to WASM: Emscripten compiles C/C++ to WebAssembly with emscripten glue code. The emcc command generates .wasm + .js loader. Flags: -O3 (optimization), -s WASM=1 (enable wasm), -s EXPORTED_FUNCTIONS (control API surface). For Rust, wasm-pack is the standard tool — it compiles Rust to wasm via wasm32-unknown-unknown target and generates npm packages. wasm-bindgen provides JS↔Rust interop. wasm-pack build --target web for web targets, --target nodejs for Node.js. AssemblyScript compiles TypeScript-like syntax to wasm. Go 1.21+ has direct wasm support via GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm.

WebAssembly JavaScript API: The WebAssembly JavaScript API provides WebAssembly.instantiate() and WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming() to compile and instantiate .wasm modules. The API returns both a Module (compiled code) and an Instance (stateful module with imports and exports). WebAssembly.compile() and WebAssembly.instantiate() are the lower-level two-phase API. WebAssembly.validate() checks if bytes are valid wasm. Imports are passed as an object with module names and import names. Exports include functions, memories, tables, and globals — accessed as properties of the instance. WebAssembly.Memory can be created externally and shared between instances.
WASM Performance Profiling: WebAssembly performance can be profiled with browser DevTools. Chrome DevTools shows wasm functions in the Performance panel with source maps for debugging. Firefox shows wasm in the Debugger with WAT disassembly. Key performance characteristics: wasm modules load and parse faster than JavaScript (binary format). Execution is typically 10-50% faster than JavaScript for CPU-intensive workloads. performance.now() measures execution time. Wasm has predictable performance — no JIT warmup or garbage collection pauses. console.time and console.timeEnd work across the JS↔wasm boundary. Large data transfer between JS and wasm can be a bottleneck — minimize crossing the boundary.
WASI & Server-Side WASM: WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) extends wasm beyond browsers to run on servers and edge runtimes. WASI provides POSIX-like syscalls: file I/O, sockets, clocks, environment variables. wasmtime (Rust), wasmer, and wazero (Go) are popular WASI runtimes. wasmtime serve creates an HTTP server from a WASI module. Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute@Edge, and Fermyon Spin use WASI for serverless-edge computing. WASI modules are sandboxed by default — access to system resources is capability-based. wasm-pack can generate WASI-compatible modules. WASI preview 2 introduces component model for better interoperability.
